text: A new AMI release for an EKS managed node group. With an EKS optimized AMI the latest security patches and operating system updates come with the latest AMI release version, and only when an update of the node group is started.

Set `release_version` on the `aws_eks_node_group` (or the module input that feeds it, for example `ami_release_version` in terraform-aws-modules/eks). It is an in-place update. When `release_version` is omitted the node group gets the latest AMI only at creation or at the next Kubernetes version change.
Set `ReleaseVersion` on the `AWS::EKS::Nodegroup` (Update requires: No interruption). No other property of the node group may change in the same update.

Set `releaseVersion` in the node group's options. `forceUpdate` defaults to true in CDK: after the 15-minute drain timeout the update ignores pod disruption budgets unless the code sets `forceUpdate: false`.
The update starts when the change is applied or the stack deploys; there is no maintenance window. EKS creates a new launch template version, scales up, then replaces the nodes.

Every node is replaced, `maxUnavailable` at a time (default one node). Pods are drained and pod disruption budgets are honoured unless the update is forced. If pods don't leave a node within 15 minutes the update fails with `PodEvictionFailure`; a node that takes more than 15 minutes to join makes it time out.

These properties replace the whole node group: `AmiType`, `CapacityType`, `ClusterName`, `DiskSize`, `InstanceTypes`, `NodegroupName`, `NodeRole`, `RemoteAccess`, `Subnets`. A move from an AL2 to an AL2023 AMI type is such a replacement, not a release bump.
The node group's version can't be greater than the control plane's. Check pod disruption budgets allow a node to drain, and that there is capacity for the extra nodes the update launches.
A failed update leaves a mixed group. To go back, update the node group again to the previous release version; nodes are replaced the same way.

EKS stopped publishing Amazon Linux 2 EKS optimized AMIs on November 26, 2025, and Kubernetes 1.32 is the last version with them. An AL2 node group has no newer release to move to: it needs AL2023 or Bottlerocket, which for a node group without a custom-AMI launch template is a new node group, not this change.
The instances run an AMI that predates the fix. The code change is a newer AMI in a new launch template version; the instances get it only when they are replaced.

Change only `image_id` on the launch template. Resolving AWS's public AMI parameter with `data "aws_ssm_parameter"` puts a concrete AMI id in a new launch template version at plan time, which keeps instance refresh, skip matching and rollback working. If the AMI comes from `data "aws_ami"` with `most_recent = true` the code is already current: change nothing and say so.

An AMI change rolls instances only when the Auto Scaling group has an `instance_refresh` block and its launch template `version` is a number or a computed value, not the literal `$Latest`. Without the block, running instances keep the old AMI until they are replaced for another reason. Terraform does not wait for the refresh to finish, and a second apply cancels a running refresh.

CloudFormation refreshes instances only when the group's `LaunchTemplate` property changes and the group has an `UpdatePolicy` (`AutoScalingInstanceRefresh` or `AutoScalingRollingUpdate`). A rolling update does not honour the group's instance maintenance policy and does not launch before terminating.

An instance refresh replaces instances in batches. With the default 90 percent minimum healthy and 100 percent maximum, 10 percent of capacity is replaced at a time and instances are terminated before new ones launch, so a small group loses an instance at a time. Minimum and maximum both at 100 percent launches before terminating.

An instance refresh can be rolled back only while it is in progress, only when it was started with a desired configuration, and not when the group uses the `$Latest` or `$Default` launch template version or an AMI alias from Parameter Store. After it finishes, start a new refresh with the previous launch template version.

Amazon Linux 2 reached its end of support on 2026-06-30 and no longer receives standard security updates: for an AL2 AMI the fix is a move to Amazon Linux 2023, which is a migration, not an AMI bump. An AL2023 AMI is locked to a repository version and does not pick up updates by itself.

The function runs a deprecated runtime: Lambda may no longer apply security updates to it. Patch-level runtime updates are applied by Lambda automatically; moving to a new major language version means changing the runtime identifier, which AWS never does for you.
Change `runtime` on the `aws_lambda_function`. If an `aws_lambda_runtime_management_config` sets `update_runtime_on = "Manual"` for the function, the runtime can't be updated until that mode changes.
Change `Runtime` on the `AWS::Lambda::Function` (Update requires: No interruption). In Serverless Framework the runtime is `provider.runtime` or the function's own `runtime`.

The change applies to `$LATEST` as soon as it is deployed. CloudFormation updates configuration and code with two calls in sequence, so invocations between them can fail; invoking through a version or alias avoids that.
`Runtime` is not a replacement property. `FunctionName` and `PackageType` are.

AWS does not guarantee backward compatibility between major language versions. Check the handler code, dependencies packaged with the function, and every layer: a layer built for one language version or operating system needs a new version built for the target runtime, and the function's layer list changes in the same pull request.

Before the old runtime's block-update date, setting the runtime back works. After it, a function can still move to a supported runtime and can't go back. AWS recommends function versions and aliases so a rollback is repointing the alias.

A function on a deprecated runtime keeps running, without security updates. After the block-create date new functions can't use the runtime, and after the block-update date the function's code and configuration can't be updated without also changing the runtime.
Non-production first: AWS Well-Architected says patching should not be performed on production systems without first testing in a safe environment.

CoderHelm ran no plan: it holds no cloud credentials. In the plan JSON a replacement shows as `change.actions` of `["delete","create"]` or `["create","delete"]`, with `replace_paths` naming the attribute. The plan for this change must show an in-place update of the one resource and nothing destroyed. If it shows "must be replaced" or a destroy, do not apply.

CoderHelm created no change set: it holds no cloud credentials. In a change set a replacement shows as `Replacement: True` (or `Conditional`), and `PolicyAction` says what happens to the old resource. An update that needs "Some interruptions" shows `Replacement: False` and still restarts the resource. If the change set shows a replacement or a removal, do not execute it.

CoderHelm ran no `cdk diff`: it holds no cloud credentials. `cdk diff` creates a change set to show accurate replacement information (or falls back to a template comparison that over-reports replacements). If it shows the resource being replaced or removed, do not deploy.

Find out how this repository applies changes before merging. Some pipelines apply on merge (a push workflow, HCP Terraform, CloudFormation Git sync, CDK Pipelines), where the plan seen in review is advisory and is recomputed; Atlantis applies from the pull request before merge. CoderHelm opens the pull request and stops there: it never applies.
